_notes: Chapters and elections. E3 §3.6–3.7, §14: the talk before the vote, the ballots, the ambition inversion, confirmation, declining, the morning after, the offices held. Order-agnostic.

events.title: Your First Chapter
events.body: The house is in chapter to elect a prior and it is the first election you have had a vote in. Nobody has said a name. The constitutions forbid campaigning and the house obeys them the way houses do, which is by talking about the weather in a tone that means a man. {@old_friar} has said twice this week that the house needs someone who can sing. {@confrere} has said that it needs someone who can read a budget. Both are describing men, and you can name them, and so can everyone.

choices.label: Ask the old man, plainly, whom he means
choices.outcome: He is delighted, and tells you, for an hour, and tells you why, and it is a real account of what the house needs and you vote his way, and the man is elected, and is good, and the old man says at supper that the young men are learning.

choices.label: Vote your own mind and say nothing to anyone
choices.outcome: The count is close. The man you voted for loses by two, and nobody knows how you voted, and the old man looks at you at supper as though he does, and the new prior is fine, and you learn how the house decides.

choices.label: Speak in the discussion: what the house needs, in your own words
choices.outcome: You are the youngest man to speak in a decade. Some of the old men are impressed and some are not, and the man you described is elected, and he knows who described him, and it is the beginning of a reputation that has two edges.

events.title: The Night Before the Ballot
events.body: The election is in the morning and the house is doing what houses do the night before: not talking about it, intensely. Recreation is subdued. {@confrere} has walked with you in the garden and said, without saying it, that men have been speaking of you, and that he does not know whether you want it, and that if you do not you should let it be known tonight, quietly, and that if you do you should let nothing be known at all.

choices.label: Let it be known, tonight, that you would rather not
choices.outcome: He tells two men and they tell four. In the morning your name draws three votes instead of, he says afterward, eleven, and the man elected is a good one, and you sleep, and the province writes down that you were asked and said no, which is not nothing.

choices.label: Say nothing at all
choices.outcome: You say nothing. In the morning your name draws seven on the first ballot and nine on the second and the house narrows, and whether you are elected is the morning's business, and you did nothing to make it so, which the house will remember either way.

choices.label: Tell him you would serve, if asked, and let him do with that what he likes
choices.outcome: He does nothing with it, being a friend, and it is known anyway by breakfast, since houses know, and your name draws what it draws and a little less, and the province writes down that you were willing, which is a heavier sentence.

events.title: The Man Who Counts Votes
events.body: There is a friar in every province who counts votes, and in this one it is {@old_friar}, who has counted them for thirty years and is usually within two. He has asked you to walk with him. He says, in the orchard, that the observant men will vote for one name and the others for another and that neither has a majority and that the eleven men in the middle will decide it, and that four of them listen to you, and that he would like to know what you will tell them.

choices.label: Tell him whom you favour, and let him carry it
choices.outcome: He carries it. The eleven move, most of them, and the man is elected on the third ballot, and the old man says at supper that it was the middle that did it, and looks at you, and the province has learned you can move a bloc, which is a thing it will remember at every chapter after.

choices.label: Say you will tell them nothing; the chapter is not a market
choices.outcome: He is not offended. He says the chapter is exactly a market and always has been, and that men who say otherwise are counted too, and the vote goes how it goes, and he is within two, as usual.

choices.label: Ask him whom he is counting for
choices.outcome: He tells you, since you asked, and it is a man you had not considered, and his reasons are good, and you tell the four, and the man is elected, and the old man never says whose bloc it was, and neither do you.

events.title: The Morning After
events.body: You were elected yesterday and this morning you are the same man in the same cell with a different name on the door, and a house of men who voted for you, and against you, waiting at the table to see what you will be. The former prior has left the keys on the desk with a list: the roof, the procurator's temper, the man who drinks, the parish's debt. The bell for Lauds is in twelve minutes and you have not decided whether to sit in the prior's stall.

choices.label: Take the prior's stall, and the bell, and the list, this morning
choices.outcome: The house sees you in the stall and something settles. The list takes four years and you get through six of its nine items, and the man who drinks is the one you do not, and you carry that.

choices.label: Keep your own stall for a week and let the house get used to it
choices.outcome: The house does not get used to it. The old men think it is false humility and the young men think it is real, and both are a little right, and on the eighth day you move, and it is noticed that you waited.

choices.label: Go to the former prior's cell before Lauds and ask him about the list
choices.outcome: He is glad to be asked and tells you everything, including the two items not on it, and it is the beginning of a working friendship the house does not expect between a man and his successor, and it helps.

events.title: The First Thing a Prior Does
events.body: Two weeks in office and the first thing that cannot be delegated: the procurator has found that {@confrere} has been using the house's account for a family matter, small sums, over a year, and has come to you with the book, and you are the prior, and the constitutions say what a prior does, and the man is at the table tonight, and he was at your profession.

choices.label: Do what the constitutions say: the warning, in writing, and the provincial informed
choices.outcome: It is correct. He is ashamed and stays and is a better friar for it, in time, and never quite easy with you, and the house learns in the first month that the new prior keeps the constitutions, which it needed to learn.

choices.label: Handle it privately: the book set right, the man spoken to, nothing written
choices.outcome: He weeps and repays it from Mass stipends over a year and is grateful for the rest of his life, and the provincial, at the visitation, finds nothing, and you have kept a thing from him in your first month, and it sits in you.

choices.label: Bring it to the house council, as the constitutions also allow
choices.outcome: The council decides, which is what councils are for, and it is the warning in writing, and it is the council's, and the man knows it was the council's and forgives you for it, and the council does not forgive you for making them.

events.title: The Floor of the Chapter
events.body: The provincial chapter, second day, and a matter on the floor that is not the election: whether the province should keep the house of studies or send its students to another province's. The observant men say a province without a studium is a mission; the others say a studium of six students is a vanity. You have a vote. You have, the chair has just said, the floor, since your hand was up before you knew it was.

choices.label: Speak to keep the studium: the province forms its own or it is not a province
choices.outcome: The room is silent and then not. The vote is close and the studium is kept, for now, and your name is attached to it, so that when it closes eleven years later someone will say you kept it open too long.

choices.label: Speak to send the students away: six students and eleven professors is not a school
choices.outcome: The old professors do not forgive it. The vote is close and the students are sent, and the province's men are formed elsewhere for a generation and come back different, and some say better, and you said it first.

choices.label: Ask a question instead: what the studium costs, and what the other province would charge
choices.outcome: Nobody knows. The chair adjourns the question to the finance committee, which is what questions like yours do, and the studium is kept another four years by default, and men remember you as the one who asked what it cost.

events.title: Asked Again
events.body: You declined the office when the chapter elected you, and the province honoured it, and now, years later, the chapter has elected you again, and the constitutions are clear about the second refusal: it ends the question for good. The provincial has telephoned himself. He says the province does not usually ask twice. He says he is not telling you what to do. He says the men who voted for you the second time knew you had declined the first, and voted anyway.

choices.label: Accept
choices.outcome: You accept. The years are what they are. The province says afterward that the best superiors are the ones who were dragged, and it is a saying with more truth than most, and you are dragged, and it is, in the end, a good term.

choices.label: Decline again, and end the question
choices.outcome: The question ends. Some of the men who voted for you twice do not speak to you for a year; the ones who understand do, and are fewer. You are a friar for the rest of your life with a door shut behind you, and there is a peace in it and a cost, and you knew both.

events.title: The Letter From the Provincial
events.body: The chapter elected you. The provincial has not confirmed it. The letter came this morning, and it is courteous and short, and it says that after consultation with his council he is unable to confirm the election and that the chapter will meet again, and it does not say why, and the house knows why, since the house has been watching you and the provincial for two years. It is the rarest thing in the order and it has happened to you.

choices.label: Accept it without a word, and be in your stall at the next chapter
choices.outcome: The house is astonished at the silence. The chapter elects another man and you vote for him, and the provincial, told how you took it, writes a line by hand that you do not answer, and in six years another provincial confirms you at once.

choices.label: Write to him and ask, once, for the reasons
choices.outcome: He gives them, in a letter he asks you to burn, and they are partly fair and partly not, and you burn it, and it changes nothing, and you know the shape of the thing you are to him, which is worth something.

choices.label: Appeal to the general curia
choices.outcome: It takes a year and Rome upholds the provincial, which Rome does, and you are the friar who appealed a refusal for the rest of the provincial's term, and the house is loyal and embarrassed, and the next chapter does not elect you.

events.title: The Chapter That Heard Too Much of You
events.body: The provincial chapter's third day, and you have spoken four times, and each time was good and each time was one more than the room wanted. At the break {@old_friar} sits by you with a coffee and says, to the wall, that he once knew a friar who had the best mind in the province and never held office because he could not stop showing it, and that the man is dead now, and that he was a friend of his.

choices.label: Say nothing for the rest of the chapter
choices.outcome: You say nothing for two days. It is noticed as much as the speaking was. At the election your name draws more than it would have, and less than it might, and the old man says on the drive home that you can learn, which from him is a great deal.

choices.label: Speak once more, on the thing that matters, and then stop
choices.outcome: The fifth time is the one they remember, since it was the last, and it changes a vote, and the old man says the count was worth the four before it, which is generous, and you are a man the chapter listens to and watches.

choices.label: Keep speaking; the province needs to hear it
choices.outcome: It hears it. Every day. By the election your name is a joke in the corridor, kindly, and it draws two votes, and one is your own, and the old man does not sit by you at the break again.

events.title: Your Friend's Name
events.body: The house is electing a prior and the name that is on every tongue is {@confrere}'s, and he is your friend, and he is not the best man for it, and you know that, and so, in a corner of himself, does he. He has asked you at recreation, lightly, what you think of the talk, and it is the lightness that tells you he wants an answer and is afraid of it.

choices.label: Tell him the truth: he would be unhappy in it, and the house would be too
choices.outcome: He is silent and then says he knows, and asks whether you would let it be known, and you do, carefully, and his name draws less, and another man is elected, and he is grateful in a year and not in a week.

choices.label: Back him; a friend is a friend, and the house will manage
choices.outcome: He is elected. He is unhappy in it, and the house is unhappy in him, for three years, and he comes to your cell at night to say so, and you say what you can, and it is the friendship that carries the term, barely.

choices.label: Say the house will decide, and vote your mind
choices.outcome: You vote for the other man. Your friend is elected anyway and never knows how you voted, and it does not matter and it does, and you are careful with him for years in a way he does not understand.

events.title: Prior Provincial
events.body: The chapter has elected you provincial and the head of the order has confirmed it by telegram, or whatever telegrams are now, and you are in the provincial's house with a desk and eleven files on it and a council waiting in the next room. Every friar in the province is yours to assign. Every house is yours to visit. The province's debt is yours to carry and its dead are yours to bury, and {@old_friar}, who did not vote for you, has sent a note that says only: pray, and eat.

choices.label: Begin by visiting every house before assigning anyone
choices.outcome: It takes four months. You know the province by Advent as no provincial has known it in a generation, and the first assignments are slow and good, and the council, which wanted them in September, forgives you by Easter.

choices.label: Begin with the council, and the eleven files
choices.outcome: The files are the province's wounds. You assign by Michaelmas and two of the assignments are wrong and are undone in a year, and the council says you listen, which is the thing they say about provincials who do.

choices.label: Begin with a week's retreat, alone, before anything
choices.outcome: The council is appalled and the old men are not. You come back and assign, and the assignments are the ones you would have made anyway, and you made them as a man who had prayed, which the province can tell, in time.

events.title: The First Letter You Send
events.body: The first assignment letter of your term, and it has a friar's name on it who will not want it: a good man, at a house he loves, needed at a house that is dying. You have written the letter three times. The council says send it. The constitutions say send it. The man's prior has telephoned to say the house would be broken by it, and it would, a little, and the other house is broken already.

choices.label: Send it, with a line by hand
choices.outcome: He goes. The line by hand is the thing he keeps. The dying house lives, because of him, and the house that loved him is bruised and heals, and you have learned what the letter costs the man who sends it, which no provincial forgets.

choices.label: Telephone him first, and ask
choices.outcome: He says yes before you have finished asking, since he is a good man, and the letter goes, and the province learns that the new provincial telephones, and every man expects it after, and it is a custom with costs and you keep it.

choices.label: Send another man, and let the good one stay where he is loved
choices.outcome: The other man goes and the dying house dies anyway, two years later, and you are not sure the good man would have saved it, and you are sure you did not try, and it is the first thing on the list you carry out of the office.

events.title: Seen
events.body: You did not campaign. You did, in the months before the chapter, accept every invitation to preach in the province's houses, and write the piece for the province's newsletter, and speak at the two meetings where speaking was noticed. It was all good work. {@old_friar} has said, at recreation, in front of the house, that a man who is everywhere before a chapter is usually nowhere after it, and did not look at you, and did not need to.

choices.label: Cancel the last two invitations and be in your stall until the chapter
choices.outcome: The house notices, and the old man notices, and it is late, and it is something. Your name draws what it draws. The old man says on the drive home that he was glad to see it, and that it may have been in time, and it was not, quite.

choices.label: Keep the invitations; good work is good work
choices.outcome: The work is good. The chapter elects another man, comfortably, and your name draws three votes, and a friar from another house says at the break, kindly, that you would have been elected if you had wanted it less.

choices.label: Ask the old man, in private, whether he meant you
choices.outcome: He says yes, and says why, for an hour, and it is the most useful hour of your religious life, and you thank him, and he says a man who can hear it may be worth the trouble, which is the only compliment he has.

events.title: Six and Six
events.body: The house has voted five times and the count is six and six, twice, and the constitutions say what happens now: the vote narrows to the two names, and if it is six and six again the senior man is elected, and the senior man is {@old_friar}, who is seventy-one and does not want it and is sitting very still. The other name is yours, and you did not want it either, and it is late in the afternoon, and someone has to move.

choices.label: Stand and withdraw your name, and vote for the old man
choices.outcome: The old man is elected by twelve votes and is furious and does it beautifully for three years and says at his term's end that it was the best thing that happened to him at seventy-one and the worst thing you ever did to him.

choices.label: Hold; the constitutions will decide
choices.outcome: The sixth ballot is six and six and the old man is elected by seniority and declines it, on his feet, which the constitutions allow, and the seventh ballot is yours, eleven to one, and the one was him, and he tells you so at supper, kindly.

choices.label: Ask the chair for five minutes and speak: what the house needs, and which of the two of you has it
choices.outcome: It is the best five minutes of your life in that house and the vote is nine to three for the old man, and he serves, and says afterward that he was talked into it by the man he was running against, which is a story he tells for years.

events.title: Sent to the Provincial Chapter
events.body: The house has elected its delegate to the provincial chapter and it is you. A week away at the house of studies with forty men, the election of the provincial, the acts that will govern everyone, and the house's instructions, which are that you should vote as the house would, which the house has not said, since it does not agree with itself. {@prior} has given you the house's mind on three matters and his own on four, and they are not the same.

choices.label: Vote the house's mind on everything, and say so at the chapter
choices.outcome: You are the delegate who says at the microphone that his house thinks a thing, and the chapter, which has heard from delegates who think things themselves, likes it, and the house, told, is pleased with itself.

choices.label: Vote your own mind, since a delegate is not a messenger
choices.outcome: You vote your own mind and it is, on two matters, not the house's. The house learns from the acts and is divided about it, and the prior says the constitutions are on your side and the table is not, and both are true.

choices.label: Vote the prior's mind; he has thought about it more than the house
choices.outcome: You vote his mind. The house learns, and the men who disagree with the prior learn that the delegate was the prior's, and the next delegate election is a different election, and you are not in it.

events.title: The Council's Vote
events.body: You sit on the provincial's council and tonight the council votes on an assignment that will break a friend: {@confrere}, to a house he has said he cannot live in, for a work the province needs done. The provincial is minded to send him. Three councillors agree. You are the fourth and your vote does not decide it and it is recorded, and the man will read the acts, since men do, and will see your name.

choices.label: Vote against, and say why, briefly
choices.outcome: The letter goes anyway. He reads the acts and sees your name and comes to your cell and says nothing about it and stays an hour, and it is the friendship kept at the cost of the council's regard, which was the trade.

choices.label: Vote for, since the province needs it and you would say so of any other man
choices.outcome: He reads the acts. He is correct with you for two years and then, in the third, says at a chapter that the council was right, and he is a better friar for the house, and the friendship is a different one, and real.

choices.label: Abstain, and say the friendship makes you unfit to vote
choices.outcome: The provincial says that is the first abstention on those grounds he has had and that it is the right one, and the letter goes, and the friend reads the abstention and understands it, and is grateful in a way that is also a little contempt.

events.title: The Third Ballot
events.body: Everyone knew who would be elected. The first ballot said so: twelve votes, four short, the rest scattered. The second ballot said fourteen. On the third the count is read and it is nine, and a name nobody had said has eleven, and the room does not breathe. The man who was going to win is looking at the floor. The man who is winning is looking at the wall. You are an elector, and the fourth ballot is in ten minutes, and the corridor is where it will be decided.

choices.label: Go to the corridor and find out what happened
choices.outcome: It was the three men from the mission house, who had been ignored and decided not to be, and had persuaded eight others in a single night, and you learn how it was done, and it is a lesson in the order's politics you use for thirty years.

choices.label: Stay in the room and vote for the man who was going to win
choices.outcome: He loses on the fourth ballot, fifteen to twelve, and is gracious, and the man elected is a surprise who turns out to be a good provincial, and you were on the losing side and it was the right side to have been on, and it lost.

choices.label: Move to the man who is winning; the chapter has spoken
choices.outcome: He wins on the fourth ballot, seventeen to ten, and you were one of the seventeen, and he knows it, since men do, and the man who was going to win knows it too, and it is remembered at the next chapter, where you are elected to nothing.

events.title: The Last Chapter of Your Term
events.body: The house is in chapter to elect your successor and you are in the prior's stall for the last time, chairing an election in which you may not be a candidate, since the term was your second. The talk before the vote has been about what the house needs next, in front of you, kindly and not, and {@confrere} has just said that the house needs a man who will listen more, and the room did not disagree, and you are the chair.

choices.label: Thank him for it, from the chair, and mean it
choices.outcome: The room is astonished and then moved. The man elected listens more, and says at his first chapter that he learned it from watching you learn it in your last, and it is the best sentence said about your term.

choices.label: Say nothing; the chair does not answer the floor
choices.outcome: The chair does not. The election proceeds. The man elected listens more, and the house remembers that you did not, and it is fair, and you carry it into the ranks with the rest.

choices.label: Answer him: what you heard, and why you did what you did
choices.outcome: It is a good answer and the wrong moment, and the room hears a prior defending his term from the chair, and the man elected is the one who said listen, and you were the one who proved it.

events.title: A Man Asks for Your Vote
events.body: The constitutions forbid it and {@confrere} has done it anyway: in the garden, before the chapter, he has asked for your vote, for himself, with reasons, well put, and a promise about the horarium that he knows you care about. He is a good man and would be a decent prior and he has just broken the one rule about elections the order actually keeps, and he knows it, and is looking at you to see whether it worked.

choices.label: Tell him you will not say, and that he should not have asked
choices.outcome: He is ashamed and says so, and you vote for him anyway, since he would be a decent prior, and never tell him, and he is elected, and keeps the promise about the horarium, and never asks anyone again.

choices.label: Say yes; the promise is a good one
choices.outcome: He is elected. He keeps the promise. Two men saw the garden, and the house knows the election had a conversation in it, and the next election has several, and the rule that was kept is not, and you were at the start of that.

choices.label: Tell the outgoing prior that you were asked
choices.outcome: The prior speaks to him, and it is a warning in words, and his name draws fewer votes than it would have, and another man is elected, and the friend knows who told, and it is a decade before the garden is forgotten.

events.title: Confirming an Election
events.body: You are provincial and a house has elected a prior you do not trust: a good friar, a poor administrator, a man who lost a house's money once in circumstances the file describes. The constitutions give you the confirmation and the refusal. The house elected him by fourteen to two. Your council is divided. A refusal is the rarest thing in the order and the house would not forget it, and neither would the man, and neither, you suspect, would you.

choices.label: Confirm him, and send a procurator you trust to the house with him
choices.outcome: He is prior for three years and the procurator keeps the books and the house is well run and the man knows why the procurator came, and thanks you for it in the fourth year, which you had not expected.

choices.label: Refuse the confirmation, and write to the house why
choices.outcome: The house is silent for a month and then elects another man, and the refused man is at your door in a year, not angry, asking what he could do, and you tell him, and he does it, and the next house that elects him you confirm.

choices.label: Delay: ask the house to meet again in a month, and say nothing about why
choices.outcome: The house understands what a delay means and elects the same man again, sixteen to nothing, and you confirm him, since a province cannot fight a house that has said a thing twice, and it was the worst of the three, and it worked.

events.title: The Vote on a Novice
events.body: The house chapter has been asked, as the constitutions require, whether a novice should be admitted to profession, and the novice is one you have taught this year, and the novice master has spoken for him, and {@old_friar} has spoken against him, quietly, on a matter of temperament the old man has watched at forty professions. The vote is by secret ballot. The novice is in the chapel, praying, since he knows what day it is.

choices.label: Vote for him
choices.outcome: He is professed by one vote and it is, in time, a good profession, and the old man was wrong, and says so at the young man's ordination, and it is the only time anyone hears him say it.

choices.label: Vote against him, since the old man has seen forty
choices.outcome: He is held a year and professed the next, better, and never knows who voted against him, and the old man says nothing and nods at you once in the cloister, and the young man is a friar for fifty years.

choices.label: Abstain, and tell the novice master you did
choices.outcome: He is disappointed. The vote passes without you. The novice is professed and is fine, and the novice master says, later, that a man who abstains on a profession has told the house he does not know what a friar is, and it stings because it may be true.

events.title: The Meeting in the Parlour
events.body: The night before the provincial chapter, in a parlour of the house of studies, eleven men are meeting to agree on a name, and you have been asked to the parlour, which means someone has counted you as one of the eleven. It is not forbidden, exactly. It is not what the constitutions mean. The men in the parlour are good men who have decided the province needs a certain provincial and intend to elect him, and they would like your vote and your friends' votes, and the tea is very good.

choices.label: Sit down, and give the name your vote and your friends'
choices.outcome: The name is elected on the second ballot and everyone in the parlour knows who was in it, and so, within a year, does everyone else, and you are a man of that bloc for the rest of your life in the province, which has advantages and a smell.

choices.label: Sit down, listen, and promise nothing
choices.outcome: You listen. You vote for the name anyway, since the reasons were good, and nobody in the parlour knows whether you did, and you are a man they invite and do not count on, which is the position you wanted.

choices.label: Thank them for the tea and leave before the name is said
choices.outcome: Two men follow you out. The name is elected anyway. The parlour knows you left and the chapter knows you were asked, and the second is worth more than the first cost, and the old men say you did it right.

events.title: The Bishop's Man at Chapter
events.body: The provincial chapter is electing, and the bishop of the diocese where the province has its parish has let it be known, through a monsignor who is somehow at the coffee, which friar he would prefer to see as provincial, since that friar has been easy to deal with. It is improper. It is also information. The old men are furious and the practical men have written the name down, and the monsignor has asked you, since you are from that diocese, what you think.

choices.label: Tell the monsignor, courteously, that the chapter elects its own
choices.outcome: He is not offended; he expected it. The bishop hears that a friar from his own diocese said it, and is displeased, and the chapter elects another man, and the province thinks well of you, and the chancery does not.

choices.label: Hear him out; the bishop's preference is a fact about the world
choices.outcome: It is. The bishop's friar is elected, narrowly, and is easy to deal with, and the parish is safe for four years, and the old men say the chapter was bought with a coffee, which is unjust, and not entirely.

choices.label: Tell the chair, before the ballot, that the diocese has expressed a preference
choices.outcome: The chair announces it, drily, and the bishop's friar draws four votes fewer than he would have, since friars do not like to be told, and the bishop hears who told, and it is a decade before you are asked to a chancery dinner.

events.title: The Man Who Was Not Elected
events.body: You were not elected. You had not sought it, and it was not expected, and your name drew nine votes on the second ballot and four on the third, and the man elected is a good man and is at the head of the table tonight, and you are at your place, and the house is watching, since the house watches this most of all: how a man is the morning after he was nearly a prior.

choices.label: Be the first to offer him whatever the house needs from you
choices.outcome: He is startled and then grateful, and gives you the work you are best at, and the house says, in the way houses do, that the man who lost was the better man and was better for losing, and both halves of that are true.

choices.label: Be exactly as you were; the vote was the vote
choices.outcome: The house watches for a month and finds nothing to see and stops, and it is right, and the man elected never knows whether you minded, and you did, a little, and it passes, as the old men said it would.

choices.label: Ask, quietly, who the nine were
choices.outcome: You find out. It was not who you thought. Two men you had counted on were not among them and one you had not was, and the knowledge is useless and you carry it to every meal for a year.

events.title: The Order Elects Its Head
events.body: The general chapter across the world is electing the head of the order and the house follows it the way a house can: a telephone call from the province's delegate each evening, written on the board. Ballot one: nine names. Ballot three: four. Ballot five: two men, one from a province like yours and one from a continent where the order is growing, and the house, at recreation, has divided along a line it did not know it had.

choices.label: Say the order should be led from where it is growing
choices.outcome: The man from the growing continent is elected on the seventh ballot and the old men are quiet and the young men are not, and the order changes under him, and the province is asked for men it does not have and gives them.

choices.label: Say the order should be led by a man who knows what it has been
choices.outcome: The man from the old province is elected on the seventh ballot and the young men are quiet and the old men are not, and the order changes less, and the province is left alone, mostly, which some call peace.

choices.label: Say the house should pray for both and vote for neither, since it cannot
choices.outcome: The house laughs and prays, and one of the two is elected, and the house says the Te Deum, and the old man says you sound like a provincial already, and does not mean it kindly, and you are not sure he is wrong.
